design_detail: Commentary in Psychedelics (vol. 2, 2025, article 100002, three pages; received 14 March, revised 13 July, accepted 30 July, available online 5 August 2025; open access, CC BY) by Elliot Marseille (UC Berkeley, Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics) and Jennifer Mitchell (San Francisco VA Medical Center; University of California San Francisco), critiquing the Lykos-funded cost-effectiveness analysis of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD by Stanicic et al. (2024, PLoS One), which was not read. Besides argument, it reports new runs of the authors' own earlier model (Marseille et al., 2020, 2022) as single numbers, without the model's structure, inputs, tables or uncertainty analysis. 13 references. Paragraph numbers in the locators count running-text paragraphs within each printed section.
can_establish: What two authors of earlier cost-effectiveness models of MDMA-assisted therapy, both with declared financial ties to the sponsor, argue about the sponsor-funded analysis: that its comparator, its drug price, its scope of costs and its threshold drive its result.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy is cost-effective: the sponsor's analysis is described rather than reproduced, the authors' new figures are reported without their model or its uncertainty, and none of the sources it uses compares MDMA-assisted therapy with standard treatments in a trial.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary on a modelling study). The analysis critiqued drew its health outcomes and PTSD-care use from trial data, with 17 months of follow-up from MAPP2 and its long-term extension (MPLONG), as the commentary states.
sample.selection_effects: The sponsor's model is compared only with the authors' own models; no economic evaluation by anyone else is cited. Several factual statements rest on news or trade sources (the FDA decision on a CNN report; Lykos's fundraising on a Lucid News article; therapist shortages on a Psychedelic Alpha piece).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Trial and model conditions as the commentary describes them: three MDMA sessions, each with two clinicians for 8 hours, within a course of therapy; the sponsor's model priced the drug at 12,000 US dollars per dose for three doses (36,000 for the drug alone, therapy not included), and costed the whole treatment at 48,376 dollars, against 11,537 dollars in the authors' 2022 model (pp. 1-2). No amounts of MDMA are given.

comparison.controls: The sponsor's model compared MDMA-assisted therapy with the same therapy given with placebo. The authors' own models use standard of care as the comparator, which in their base case carries no new costs and no change in health status (p. 1).

outcomes.instruments: Incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY); time to break even for payers; dominance (lower cost with better health).
outcomes.operationalization: Cost-effectiveness judged against willingness-to-pay thresholds of 150,000 US dollars per QALY (the sponsor's analysis) and about 100,000 (preferred by the authors).

analysis.effect_sizes: As stated, without intervals: sponsor's model, about 84,000 US dollars per QALY for MDMA-assisted therapy versus placebo-therapy over five years. Authors' model: break-even at 3.8 years in their 2022 analysis at a much lower drug price; about 8.4 years with the sponsor's 36,000-dollar drug cost; 160 dollars per QALY over five years with the drug priced at 10,500 dollars for the course; dominant at any drug cost below 10,320 dollars; a drug price about 12% lower would allow therapists' hourly rate to rise from 147 to 200 dollars.
analysis.selective_reporting: The new model runs are reported without methods, inputs or sensitivity analyses. The sponsor's analysis is credited with trial-based estimates and a documented fall in health-care use without any of its numbers other than the ratio, the threshold and the prices.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Arithmetic and model outputs showing that, in these models, the result depends heavily on the drug's price and on what MDMA-assisted therapy is compared with; no new data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the sponsor's analysis methodologically rigorous but of limited relevance to decision-makers, and says alternative modelling suggests that at about 10,500 dollars MDMA therapy could be extremely cost-effective, around 160 dollars per QALY, or even cost-saving. Those figures come from the authors' own model, whose base-case comparator brings no new costs and no change in health status (p. 1); the commentary does not say how much of the improvement seen with MDMA-assisted therapy its model credits to the treatment, nor show what happens if standard care itself improves health. It notes that no head-to-head trial against standard treatments exists, yet presents its comparison with standard care as the more accurate one. Neither model, as described, allows for the possibility that the trial effect was inflated by unblinding or expectancy.

timeline.event: Marseille et al. (2015), on alternative approaches to cost-effectiveness thresholds, cited for the weakness of the WHO three-times-GDP heuristic (not read).
Marseille, Kahn, Yazar-Klosinski and Doblin (2020), cost-effectiveness of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD (cited; not read).
Marseille, Mitchell and Kahn (2022), updated cost-effectiveness using findings from a phase 3 trial: break-even for payers at 3.8 years (as stated here; not read).
FDA declines to approve MDMA-assisted therapy in August 2024, as reported by CNN (McPhillips, 2024) and cited here.
Stanicic, Zah, Grbic and De Angelo (2024), the Lykos-funded cost-effectiveness analysis critiqued here (PLoS One; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: No economic evaluation independent of both the sponsor and the authors of the earlier models is among the sources read for this batch; all the models described come from the sponsor or from authors with declared ties to it.

funding.funder: No funding was received for this commentary.
funding.declared_conflicts: Elliot Marseille has received consulting fees from MAPS PBC/Lykos. Jennifer Mitchell has received research support from MAPS PBC/Lykos.
funding.affiliations_note: Elliot Marseille: UC Berkeley, Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics; Jennifer Mitchell: Staff for Research and Development, SFVAMC, and Departments of Neurology and Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Weill Institute for Neurosciences, University of California San Francisco. The authors critique a rival analysis and offer their own models (2020, 2022; the 2022 model co-authored by both) as the alternative. The second author's name matches that of the first author of the two phase 3 trial reports (Jennifer M. Mitchell in the Crossref records of mitchell_2021 and mitchell_2023); the commentary does not mention a role in the trials. The authors declare that ChatGPT was used to edit the manuscript and to develop responses to reviewers. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cost-effectiveness analysis independent of the sponsor and of earlier modellers with ties to it, comparing MDMA-assisted therapy with the evidence-based treatments people with PTSD actually receive (using trial or indirect-comparison estimates for both, with the trials' blinding problems allowed for), counting all health-care costs, publishing its inputs and running probabilistic sensitivity analyses over a range of drug prices; ultimately, a pragmatic trial against standard care that collects costs.

domains.note: A commentary on one analysis; the only alternatives offered are the authors' own models.

The sponsor's analysis is appraised on comparator, price, scope of costs and threshold, and its strengths are acknowledged; the authors' own model is not appraised and its new outputs are unreported in method.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The alternative figures come entirely from the authors' own models (2020, 2022), and the threshold argument cites their own 2015 paper.
New model outputs are given without methods; the motives behind the sponsor's price and the possibility that some patients need fewer MDMA sessions are speculative.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the cost-effectiveness of MDMA-assisted therapy (uncertainty about the size of the trial effect under-represented)
domains.note: Both the sponsor's and the authors' models take the trials' effects at face value; that unblinding or expectancy might have inflated the effect, which would make the therapy less cost-effective, is not considered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The piece may be cited for what the cost-effectiveness question turns on as these critics state it (comparator, drug price, scope of costs, threshold, time horizon) and for its description of the sponsor's analysis, labelled as second-hand. Its own figures are outputs of a model whose inputs are not published here; they are not evidence that MDMA-assisted therapy saves money.

key_findings.finding: The analysis critiqued (Stanicic et al., 2024) was funded by Lykos Therapeutics and appeared after the FDA declined to approve MDMA-assisted therapy in August 2024 (citing a CNN report). The authors name two critical limitations: an inappropriate comparator and a pricing strategy that threatens access.

The sponsor's model compared MDMA-assisted therapy with an identical therapy regimen given with placebo, which the authors call appropriate for regulatory approval but not informative for payers, because people with PTSD usually receive evidence-based psychotherapies (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) or SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine), not placebo plus the trial's intensive therapy (described in the exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Inappropriate choice of comparator, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that head-to-head trial data against standard treatments are lacking. Their own earlier models used standard of care as comparator; in the base case the comparator carried no new costs and no change in health status, and the whole MDMA treatment cost 11,537 US dollars against 48,376 in the sponsor's model, mainly because of a much lower drug cost; this gave net savings at the five-year horizon.
key_findings.locator: Inappropriate choice of comparator, 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: The sponsor's analysis reported an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of about 84,000 US dollars per QALY for MDMA versus placebo-therapy, under its threshold of 150,000 dollars per QALY.
key_findings.locator: Inappropriate choice of comparator, 2nd paragraph (p. 1, right column, continued on p. 2, left column)

key_findings.finding: Strengths credited to the sponsor's analysis: health outcomes and PTSD-care use estimated from clinical-trial data rather than the literature, and 17 months of follow-up from the MAPP2 and MPLONG trials; a documented reduction in health-care use among people treated with MDMA. Limitation: only PTSD-specific health-care costs were counted, leaving out emergency, inpatient and comorbidity costs.
key_findings.locator: Methodological strengths despite flawed comparator, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: The authors call the 150,000-dollar threshold defensible but at the high end of values in use, weakly justified by the WHO three-times-GDP heuristic, and say about 100,000 dollars per QALY better reflects consensus; at either threshold, 84,000 dollars per QALY may not convince payers.
key_findings.locator: Methodological strengths despite flawed comparator, 3rd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Pricing: the sponsor's model priced MDMA at 36,000 US dollars for the full course of the drug, therapy excluded (the per-dose price is in the exposure field). With this drug cost in the authors' model, payers' break-even moves from 3.8 years (their 2022 analysis, at a much lower price) to about 8.4 years, beyond the average enrolment period of most US health plans. With the drug priced at 10,500 dollars for the course, their model gives 160 dollars per QALY over five years, and below 10,320 dollars treatment is dominant (better health at lower cost).
key_findings.locator: Drug pricing: a critical policy concern, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Outputs of the authors' model, reported without inputs or uncertainty intervals.

key_findings.finding: Workforce: a drug price about 12% lower would allow therapists' hourly rate to rise from 147 US dollars (the rate in the sponsor's model) to 200, which the authors argue could help recruitment and retention.
key_findings.locator: Drug pricing: a critical policy concern, 3rd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: On the sponsor: Lykos (formerly MAPS PBC), a public benefit corporation, raised over 140 million US dollars in philanthropy and more than 100 million from investors to fund the phase 3 trials and the approval process (Harrison and Jordan, 2024); bringing a drug to market is said to cost 500 million to 1 billion dollars (no source); the sponsor's analysis did not give recovery of research costs as a reason for its price, and the authors judge the price misaligned with the company's stated mission.
key_findings.locator: Drug pricing: a critical policy concern, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Policy conclusions: payers need comparisons with treatments used in practice (or at least indirect comparisons); a 36,000-dollar drug cost risks a two-tiered system; the authors suggest charging only for the MDMA sessions actually given, on the untested assumption that some patients might need fewer than the protocol's maximum; and call for models with realistic comparators, all health-care costs and balanced pricing.
key_findings.locator: Policy implications and conclusions, 2nd to 6th paragraphs (p. 2, right column, to p. 3, left column)

key_findings.finding: Declared interests: Elliot Marseille has received consulting fees from MAPS PBC/Lykos; Jennifer Mitchell has received research support from MAPS PBC/Lykos; no funding for this study. ChatGPT was used to edit the manuscript and to develop responses to reviewers.
key_findings.locator: Conflict of interest and source of funding; Declaration of Generative AI (right and left columns)

reporting_issues.issue: The new model results (break-even at about 8.4 years with the sponsor's drug cost; 160 US dollars per QALY at 10,500 dollars; dominance below 10,320 dollars; therapist rate rising from 147 to 200 dollars with a 12% lower price) are given without the model's inputs, structure or uncertainty.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be checked from the paper; cite them only as the authors' model outputs.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors reject the placebo-therapy comparator as unrealistic, but their own base-case comparator assumes no new costs and no change in health status for people receiving standard care; the paper does not report how its results change if standard care improves health, which another source in this batch reports for the psychotherapies named (effect sizes over one standard deviation; Earleywine et al., 2025, p. 1, citing Cusack et al., 2016).
reporting_issues.consequence: The more favourable figures depend on this assumption as well as on the lower price; the critique shows how sensitive the result is to the comparator, not which comparator result is right.

reporting_issues.issue: The FDA decision is dated to August 2024 from a CNN report, and the cost of bringing a drug to market (500 million to 1 billion dollars) is attributed to unnamed analysts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the regulator's own documents for the decision and its date.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-3 (PDFs/MDMA/Marseille_2025_CritiqueCostEffectiveness.pdf): read in full, including the interdisciplinarity, CRediT, generative-AI, conflict-of-interest and data-availability statements and the reference list; all three pages rendered.
